However, there have been no complaints or issues related to user acceptability. 10. Was the city encouraged by the manufacturers of adaptive lighting technology to adopt? If yes, how was this manifested? The responses varied, but overall, the manufacturers of adaptive lighting technology did not play a significant role in encouraging the cities to adopt the technology. One respondent stated that they were flooded with information from manufacturers during the process and had them fill out surveys, but there was no clear indication of encouragement. Another respondent stated that their city had a strict procurement code that prohibited conversations with vendors ahead of time. One respondent mentioned that some cities are first approached by control manufacturers, and they had a project where they did a control demonstration before conducting a lighting study. Finally, one respondent mentioned that their system had a dimming capability that came with the overall system function, and the manufacturer was responsive in helping with the operating system. 11. Was the city well supported by the manufacturers of adaptive lighting technology? If yes, what form did this support take? If no, what problems did this create? The responses to the question of whether the city was well supported by manufacturers of adaptive lighting technology were mixed. Some manufacturers were supportive and attended meetings, provided free equipment, and gave training and support. However, others had challenges in deploying the technology, such as interference and difficulty in finding suitable locations for the equipment. Some manufacturers had to make modifications to their equipment during testing. Other challenges included high costs, difficulty in replacing equipment at the end of the contract period, and the need to retrofit the next generation product. Additionally, some cities faced scaling challenges, slow central management system application, and the need to replace legacy technology. While manufacturers continue to provide support and updates, there is still resistance to the cost of retrofitting the new system. 12. How has your engagement with the electric utility assisted in the adoption and implementation of adaptive lighting technology? Responses suggest that engagement with electric utilities can vary depending on whether they are city-owned or investor-owned utilities (IOUs). While city-owned utilities may be more cooperative in implementing adaptive lighting technology, IOUs can be resistant, and there may be a need for work orders to prompt action. Some states have implemented decoupling, where IOUs can only make a profit by decreasing demand, which has led to success in adaptive 76 controls. Utility companies may have rebate programs for energy use, and some smaller utilities may be more willing to work with customers on adaptive lighting. However, implementing adaptive lighting can be a burden for both the utility company and the city or streetlight owner, and coordination can become a headache.
